title: The Incident Response Lifecycle: Detect, Triage, Mitigate, Resolve

scenes.heading: Incident Response Lifecycle
scenes.narration: Every serious incident follows a predictable lifecycle, and knowing the stages keeps a response fast and coordinated instead of chaotic.

scenes.heading: The four stages
scenes.narration: Detection is the moment a monitor or a user surfaces that something is wrong. Triage assesses severity, assigns roles, and communicates scope. Mitigation stops the bleeding fast, even with a temporary fix, and only then does resolution address the true root cause.

scenes.heading: Roles during an incident
bullets: Incident commander: coordinates, does not fix directly
Operations lead: drives the technical investigation
Scribe: records the timeline as events unfold
scenes.narration: The incident commander coordinates the response and deliberately stays hands-off so nobody loses the big picture. The operations lead drives the actual technical investigation. A communications lead shields responders by handling stakeholder updates, and a scribe captures the timeline that will power the postmortem.

scenes.heading: Mitigate vs resolve
scenes.narration: Mitigation is about restoring service as quickly as possible, and a temporary patch or rollback is perfectly acceptable. Resolution comes later, once the pressure has eased, and targets the underlying cause so the problem does not return. Confusing the two leads teams to chase perfect fixes while users keep suffering.

scenes.text: Mitigate first, resolve second. Getting service back beats a perfect root-cause fix that leaves users broken for another hour.
scenes.narration: The golden rule is to mitigate first and resolve second, because restoring service beats a perfect root-cause fix that leaves users broken for another hour.
